“Bye, Grampa.” She stared down at the bill as she left
through the back.

The back room housed the Saponofied Iroquois
Princess—a girl tuned to soap. The brass placard said that
she died two hundred years ago from heartbreak when her
lover, a Hessian general, left her to sail the high seas. She
never asked Grampa Lyssie if she was real or if he’d molded
her dark, splotchy skin with his own hands. It didn’t look
like Grampa’s work, though. Grampa always worked hard
to make his figures attractive. So did Claire, for that matter.

The walk down to the Green Store wasn’t so bad, except
that she didn’t have anything to wear that was quite warm
enough. She wondered ifa girl could really turn to soap out
of heartbreak, the pain stilling her flesh from the outside in.
She wondered what the weather was like in Jackson City
right now. She wondered whether the five note would get
her all the way to Missouri, but frowned at the thought of
making Grampa Lyssie cry again. Anyhow, it was probably
snowy and icy. Somehow, the thought didn’t make her feel
any warmer now. A chilly breeze came down from the
Mountains to fight with the dirty wafts of heat thrown off
by buildings and automobiles in town. Here, in a gully ste
used as a shortcut past the curling driveway, the cold won
out and chewed at her soul under the trees that shadowed a
al Teady overcast afternoon. As she made her Way

It's been raining here for two weeks. I gaze out of my 14" floor apartment window at the Chicago
sky, dark as a Leonard Cohen song. I guess the apartment is starting to stink. I haven't done laundry
in wer a month, and filthy clothes are strewn about the place. I haven't really noticed any smell yet—
I quit bathing last Tuesday—but the pizza delivery boy nearly passed out yesterday when I opened my
decor, | think unholy things are growing in the sink, but I don't go near the kitchenette anymore. The
garbage in there completely covers the floor and is pushing its way out onto the living room carpet.
‘The tiny bedroom has been closed off for months, making me think of a Julio Cortazar story. “House
‘Taken Over.” I try to remember how this apartment looked when we first moved in, when Allie was
still with me. I can't.

She left because of the housecoat. It was blue and tattered when we moved here, now it's little
more than a threadbare sheet with sleeves that I wrap around my nakedness.

“My god Michael, when are you going to throw out that fucking housecoat?” she asked me one
fateful Wednesday afternoon. ‘There would be no sweet loving that hump day.

I shrugged and turned back to my computer screen, hovering over the keyboard and rubbing the
comers of my lips. She picked up the remote control and muted the television. I had ceased paying
attention to it hours ago, but now that the sound was missing, I noticed it. | swiveled my chair and
frowned at her. “What.” It wasn't a question. 1 knew she was mad about ‘something, and this four-
